setupSteps: Choose the step. Use the bottom stair (in an Indian building often 15-19 cm, est.), a heavy step stool, or a gym bench. Beginners aim for about 10-15 cm; add height only when 3 sets of 8 are smooth and pain-free. If a stair is higher than about 20 cm, start with the bottom stair only, or use a lower step; do not use a normal dining chair (about 45 cm, est.).

Test stability. Press down hard on the step with your hands, then your foot. It must not rock, slide, fold, flex or tip. Do not use a step with wheels, a wobbly stool, a stack of books, a cushion, a cane chair, a plastic garden chair that flexes, or a folding step that can close.

Check the surface. Dry, non-slip floor and a non-slip step top. Wet stairs in monsoon, polished marble and stair tiles with loose edges are not safe. Wear flat shoes with grip, or go barefoot on a dry rubber mat on a floor step; no socks on smooth floors.
Place the step against a wall (stool or bench) so that it cannot slide; for a building stair, stand with a handrail or wall within light reach on the side of the rail.
Stance. Stand tall, feet hip-width apart, facing the step about one foot-length (20-30 cm, est.) away. Eyes forward, ribs down, shoulders relaxed, arms by your sides or on your hips.
Foot position. The whole foot goes on the step, heel included, toes pointing forward, knee tracking over the second toe (not caving in).
Support rule. Use the wall or rail as light balance only: fingertips, not a pull. If you have to pull to get up, the step is too high.
Lighting and space (stairs). Good light, no shoes or bags on the stairs, nobody coming down, and not in a stairwell used as a fire exit at busy times (est.).
Camera. Phone in landscape at hip height (about 80-100 cm, est.), 2 m to your side (side view), with the full step and whole body visible.
Clothing. Fitted trousers or leggings and a fitted top so the camera sees hips, knees and ankles.
Warm up for 1-2 minutes with marching on the spot and a few bodyweight squats (Home 1) to a comfortable depth.

steps.part: A. Beginner forward step-up (10-15 cm step, lead leg alternates by set)
steps.title: Stand tall facing the step
steps.action: Feet hip-width apart, about 20-30 cm (est.) from the step, hands on hips or fingertips on the wall.
steps.feel: Even weight on both feet; calm, upright.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ear, shoulder, hip and ankle roughly in a line. Front: shoulders and hips level.

steps.part: A. Beginner forward step-up (10-15 cm step, lead leg alternates by set)
steps.title: Place the lead foot
steps.action: Lift one foot and place the whole foot flat on the step, toes forward.
steps.feel: Heel and ball of the foot both pressed into the step; thigh engaged.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shin nearly upright, knee not far past the toes. Front: knee over the second toe, not falling inward.

steps.part: A. Beginner forward step-up (10-15 cm step, lead leg alternates by set)
steps.title: Lean slightly and shift weight onto the lead foot
steps.action: Lean the chest slightly forward from the hips, then move your weight over the lead foot. The rear foot stays on the floor and takes only a little weight.
steps.feel: Most of the weight in the lead heel and mid-foot.
steps.visualCheck: Side: trunk leaning only a little; hip not pushed far back.

steps.part: A. Beginner forward step-up (10-15 cm step, lead leg alternates by set)
steps.title: Press up
steps.action: Push through the lead heel and mid-foot to straighten the hip and knee and stand tall on the step. Do not push off the rear foot or bounce.
steps.feel: Thigh and bottom working on the step side.
steps.visualCheck: Side: smooth rise, no hip hitching. Front: knee and hip stay in line; pelvis stays level.

steps.part: A. Beginner forward step-up (10-15 cm step, lead leg alternates by set)
steps.title: Stand tall on the step
steps.action: Bring the rear foot up beside the lead foot or just tap it on the step; stand upright with the lead knee straight but not locked hard.
steps.feel: Tall, balanced, thigh and bottom squeezed.
steps.visualCheck: Side: knee and hip near straight (about 165 degrees or more, est.); torso upright. Front: hips level.

steps.part: A. Beginner forward step-up (10-15 cm step, lead leg alternates by set)
steps.title: Lower slowly (step-down control)
steps.action: Shift your weight onto the lead leg, then slowly lower the rear foot back to the floor, with the lead knee bending in a controlled way. Place the foot softly, toes first then heel, no stamping.
steps.feel: Thigh working to brake the descent; no wobble.
steps.visualCheck: Side: hips move back slightly, torso stays tall. Front: knee over the second toe, hips level.

steps.part: A. Beginner forward step-up (10-15 cm step, lead leg alternates by set)
steps.title: Return the lead foot
steps.action: Step the lead foot down beside the other so both feet are on the floor.

steps.part: A. Beginner forward step-up (10-15 cm step, lead leg alternates by set)
steps.title: Repeat
steps.action: Repeat from step 2 on the same leg for the planned reps (6-8 for a beginner), then change legs (or alternate legs each rep for a gentle, flowing version).
steps.feel: Smooth rhythm; stop if the knee pinches or balance wobbles.
steps.visualCheck: Same depth, tall finish and soft landing on the last rep as the first.

steps.part: A. Beginner forward step-up (10-15 cm step, lead leg alternates by set)
steps.title: Finish and rest
steps.action: Stand on the floor, shake out the legs.
steps.visualCheck: Stop for the day if a knee, hip or ankle hurts.

steps.title: Stand sideways next to the step, near foot about 10 cm (est.) from it. Put the whole near foot on the step, toes forward, knee over the second toe

Keep the chest tall and the hips square (hips face forward, not twisted). Press through the near heel to stand tall on the step, tap the far foot beside it, then lower the far foot slowly to the floor (2-3 s). The far foot touches lightly; the near leg does the work

Do all reps on one side, then switch. Starting height: 10-15 cm; lateral usually bends the knee a little more than the forward version (a study in older adults found larger peak knee bend with lateral step-up than forward, est. same direction in young adults), so keep it as low as the forward version at first
Stand on the step on one leg, other foot hovering beside it. Slowly bend the standing knee and sink down, tap the hovering heel lightly on the floor, then press back up

Lower for 3 seconds (est.), keep the knee over the second toe, hips level and trunk tall. Use a low step (10-15 cm). Use a wall or rail for light balance. This is a knee-demanding version (the forward step-down gave higher patellofemoral force than step-up at the same knee bend; abstract only). If it causes knee pain, go back to the forward step-up or a smaller height

Hold a light dumbbell in each hand at your sides (palms facing in), arms straight, shoulders down and back. Do the forward step-up exactly as in A, slower and with an upright chest. Start with weights you can control for 10-12 reps per leg (est.); a general weight-choice guide suggests small jumps of about 1-2.5 kg per dumbbell. Do not use a rail grip with dumbbells; use a lower step and a wall or no support. Stop if the weights swing or the posture slumps

commonMistakes.title: Step too high
commonMistakes.text: Step too high. Why: a step that forces the knee past about 90 degrees increases knee load, makes you pull on the rail and use the rear leg and momentum (ACE's older step guidance says knee bend should not pass 90 degrees under load; one study with aerobic steps found larger knee bend at higher steps, so people with knee issues should use low or medium steps). Fix: bottom stair or 10-15 cm step; build up slowly.

commonMistakes.title: Pushing off the back foot
commonMistakes.text: Pushing off the back foot. Why: the rear leg does the work so the lead leg is not trained, and it hides balance problems (stated in a rehab handout and several coaching sources). Fix: keep the rear foot light; push through the lead heel.

commonMistakes.title: Knee caving inward (valgus)
commonMistakes.text: Knee caving inward (valgus). Why: it is linked in clinical and coaching sources to more patellofemoral stress (the mechanism is inferred; a step-up-specific trial of how height affects valgus: Not found). Fix: cue the knee over the second toe, use a lower step, strengthen with the lateral step-up.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping down fast or stomping
commonMistakes.text: Dropping down fast or stomping. Why: the lowering phase is harder on the knee than the rising phase (step-down gave higher patellofemoral force in the lab abstract) and it is loud in a flat. Fix: count 2-3 seconds down, place the foot toes first.

commonMistakes.title: Leaning too far forward or backward
commonMistakes.text: Leaning too far forward or backward. Why: a big forward fold shifts the work to the back and hips and can strain the lower back; leaning back is unstable. Fix: small lean from the hips, chest proud.

commonMistakes.title: Pulling on the handrail
commonMistakes.text: Pulling on the handrail. Why: the arms take over and the leg is not trained. Fix: fingertip balance only, or lower the step.

commonMistakes.title: Only toes on the step or heel hanging off
commonMistakes.text: Only toes on the step or heel hanging off. Why: less stable, more load on the front of the ankle and knee (a sweat.com-style cue and commercial sources say to push through the heel; sources disagree on heel vs ball of the foot, so FitPlate uses the whole foot with weight in the heel and mid-foot). Fix: whole foot flat on the step.

commonMistakes.title: Hips hitching or dropping
commonMistakes.text: Hips hitching or dropping. Why: weak side-hip control; one hip rises or falls. Fix: slower reps, lateral step-up, lower step.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: breath-holding during effort raises blood pressure (lab data from heavy lifting, PubMed 7741618). Fix: breathe out as you rise, in as you lower.

commonMistakes.title: Using an unstable step or slippery surface
commonMistakes.text: Using an unstable step or slippery surface. Why: a fall is the main real-world risk. Fix: test the step, wall behind it, non-slip footwear, dry floor.

commonMistakes.title: Adding dumbbells too soon
commonMistakes.text: Adding dumbbells too soon. Why: weights make balance and form harder and raise the load on a knee that is not ready. Fix: add weight only after 3 x 8 per leg are smooth and pain-free at your step height, and only 1-2.5 kg per hand at a time (est.).

safetyNotes: Knee pain, knee osteoarthritis, patellofemoral (front-of-knee) pain, recent knee injury or surgery: use a very low step (about 5-10 cm), a handrail, and slow reps; avoid step-downs and higher steps until a physiotherapist approves. The lowering phase and deeper knee bend increase patellofemoral loading (abstract of Chinkulprasert et al.; a general rehab progression uses bar-assisted, then low-box step-downs while avoiding knee valgus).
Balance problems, dizziness, previous falls, or foot or ankle pain: do the exercise next to a wall or rail on the bottom step only, with a second person nearby, or choose the sit-to-stand.

High blood pressure and heart disease: keep sets short, effort at moderate 5-6/10 or lighter, no holding the breath, rise slowly; get clearance first if blood pressure is uncontrolled or you have heart disease.
Lower back pain: keep the chest tall with only a small forward lean; avoid rounding the back; stop if pain spreads down a leg.
High body weight: use a low, very sturdy step and long rests; check the step's strength (home stool weight rating: Not found).
Pregnancy, postpartum, recent surgery: ask your clinician before step-ups (balance changes in pregnancy raise fall risk).

Stairwell rules (Mumbai building): use the bottom step only, never the open edge of a landing, never a wet or dusty stair, never a stair used by others at that moment, and avoid doing it on a stair with a broken or loose edge (est.).

conditionCautions.change: Counts as strength plus light cardio; usual glucose checks and fast carbohydrate on hand if on insulin or sulfonylureas; check feet and footwear if neuropathy
After clearance only: low step, short sets, steady breathing; stop with chest discomfort, breathlessness or dizziness
conditionCautions.source: AHA physical activity recommendations; step-up-specific clearance Not found

conditionCautions.change: Counts toward the resistance part of the weekly mix; aerobic minutes still come from other items

conditionCautions.change: Fits general strength and aerobic guidance; no step-up-specific advice found

conditionCautions.change: Very low step (about 5-10 cm), rail support, slow lowering; skip step-downs and dumbbells until a physiotherapist agrees; stop with sharp or increasing knee pain

Weight-bearing strength work is encouraged; low step with a rail, tall spine, avoid fall risk; get individual advice especially after a fracture
